title: SQL-like or RQB: authors with their posts
description: Load the same authors with a join and a relational query, then compare the results you get.

steps.label: Two APIs
steps.title: Load authors with their posts
steps.body:
You need authors and their posts for a page. Drizzle gives you two APIs: the **SQL-like query builder**, with `select` and joins, and the **relational query builder (RQB)**, with `db.query` and `with`. Both sides here use Drizzle ORM **1.0.0-rc.5** and the same data.

On the SQL-like side, `leftJoin` connects each post's `authorId` to a user's `id`. On the RQB side, `with: { posts: ... }` uses the relations declared in `schema.ts`. Those relations describe how tables connect; the foreign key in the schema enforces the link in the database.

Press **Run**. Compare **Joined rows** on the SQL-like side with **Authors with posts** on the RQB side. The data is the same, but its shape differs.

meta.summary: One join and one relational query load the same data.
meta.changed: The join returned four rows. RQB returned three authors, each with a posts array.

steps.label: Two posts
steps.title: Why does Ada appear twice?
steps.body:
Ada wrote **Hello, Drizzle** and **Joins without the boilerplate**. The join returns one row for each matching user and post, so Ada's name appears twice. `select` chooses `userId`, `name` and `title` for each row.

RQB returns Ada once, with both titles inside her `posts` array. `columns` chooses the fields at each level: `name` for the user, `title` for each post.

Both queries order by user ID and post ID, so you can compare the same records in the same order.

meta.summary: Two joined rows become one author with two nested posts.

steps.label: No posts
steps.title: Keep Linus, even without a post
steps.body:
Linus has no posts. The **left join** still returns his user row, with `title: null` because no post matched. An `innerJoin` would leave him out.

RQB also keeps Linus, with `posts: []`. Asking for posts with `with` does not require the user to have any.

For an author card, that empty array is useful: you can show the author's name and an empty state without removing the author from the page.

meta.summary: No matching post means a null title in the join and an empty array in RQB.

steps.label: Same shape
steps.title: Build the same nested result
steps.body:
You can return nested authors from the SQL-like query too. The query stays the same; the new code groups its rows in JavaScript.

The `Map` keeps one author per **user ID**, so two people with the same name stay separate. Each non-null title becomes a post. Linus still gets an author entry, but the null check leaves his posts array empty.

Press **Run**, then compare **Authors with posts** on both sides. The results now match. RQB already did this grouping for you.

meta.summary: Group the joined rows by user ID to match the RQB result.
meta.changed: Both sides returned Ada with two posts, Grace with one, and Linus with an empty posts array.

steps.label: Which API?
steps.title: Choose the result your page needs
steps.body:
For a report with one row per author and post, the **SQL-like query** already returns the shape you need. You choose the selected fields and the join condition directly.

For author cards with a list of posts under each name, **RQB** returns that nested shape through your declared relations. You choose the fields and related records without writing the grouping loop.

You can use both APIs in the same application. Choose per query, based on the result you need. Here, both approaches returned the same authors and posts; the difference was who assembled the nested objects.

meta.summary: Flat rows for a report; nested authors for cards with posts.
